name: Agent detection
statement: People read ambiguous movement and sound as the work of an agent, and cognitive scientists of religion proposed that this habit is what seeds belief in gods and spirits.
meaning: Two claims travel under one name and they have separate evidence. The first is that a system for spotting other creatures fires on thin evidence, because missing a predator costs more than a false alarm. The second is that these false alarms encourage belief in supernatural agents, so that religion is partly a by-product of a jumpy detector. Justin Barrett named the device and made the second claim the engine of an explanation of religion. The device has a specific prediction attached: threat and ambiguity should push detection up. That prediction is testable, has been tested, and is where most of the trouble is. Pareidolia, entry no. 33, and apophenia, entry no. 41, are separate entries, and both are narrower. Pareidolia is a false positive in face perception; apophenia is meaning found in noise of any kind. Agent detection is about attributing a purposeful actor, which is neither a face nor a pattern.

origin.note: Barrett's review of the new cognitive science of religion is where the device gets its name. The idea is older. Stewart Guthrie's Faces in the Clouds, published by Oxford University Press in 1993, argued that people take the human model as a default and read humanness into the world. Maij, van Schie and van Elk trace the lineage and record that Barrett in 2000 proposed an agent detection device, renamed an agency detection device in 2004 to cover the intentional aspect. Barrett's own 2000 abstract does not mention the device, and the full text could not be opened on 21 September 2026, so the naming is stated on Maij and colleagues' authority rather than read at source.

evidence:
The laboratory basis is Heider and Simmel's 1944 film of two triangles and a disc moving around a rectangle. Three groups of undergraduate women watched it, 34 in the first experiment, 36 in the second and 44 in the third. Given only the instruction to write down what happened, all but one of the 34 read the movements as actions of animate beings, in most cases persons and in two cases birds. The exception described the shapes almost entirely in geometrical terms. Even her report slipped into calling the large triangle 'he', which the authors mark with a 'sic'. The paper's summary adds that every subject in the second group, and all but two in the third, saw animated beings as well. The attribution of purpose to moving geometry is the most robust thing in this literature.

The belief link was then tested in two directions. Van Elk's 2013 study used a point-light biological motion task on skeptics and paranormal believers. Believers had lower perceptual sensitivity, driven by a bias to answer yes when no agent was present, and the difference held only at low to intermediate ambiguity. The same paper reports that illusory agency detection was unrelated to traditional religious belief and to belief in witchcraft. Riekki, Lindeman and Raij scanned 12 believers and 11 skeptics watching moving shapes, and believers rated random movement as more intentional with stronger activation in medial prefrontal circuitry.

Van Elk, Rutjens, van der Pligt and van Harreveld ran five experiments priming people with words for supernatural agents before biological motion or face and house judgements, with 40, 35, 35, 20 and 36 students plus 60 visitors to a Dutch paranormal fair. Human primes helped agency detection. Supernatural primes produced no general effect, and moderation by religiosity appeared in three of the experiments.

Andersen, Pfeiffer, Müller and Schjoedt put people in a virtual forest in a preregistered study and told them to detect beings. Participants expecting a high probability of an encounter made many more false detections than those expecting a low probability, and degrading sensory reliability raised the false detection rate by much less. Expectation, not threat, moved the needle.

examples.text: A house settles and the sleeper hears someone moving about. What arrives is not a face or a pattern but a being with intentions, and it arrives before any of the ordinary causes are considered.

examples.tag: The shapes moving on a screen
examples.text: Two triangles and a circle move about a diagram, and viewers describe a chase, a bully and an escape. Purpose attributed to bare motion is the settled half of the claim, and the easiest half to reproduce.

examples.tag: The undergrowth that shifts in a wood
examples.text: A walker sees a branch move and reacts as though something is there, then finds the wind. The false alarm costs a moment of fright, and the account is built on how much the opposite error would cost.

replication.headline: Six experiments designed to make people over-detect agents failed to do so, and neither religiosity nor paranormal belief predicted the response bias, while one earlier study of paranormal believers had found exactly that bias.
replication.detail:
Maij, van Schie and van Elk ran six threat-inducing experiments, the first direct test of the assumption that threatening ambiguity drives agent detection up. They recruited 233 people, 30, 33, 31, 63, 45 and 31 across the six, and analysed fewer in three of them after exclusions. Threat came from International Affective Picture System images, then classical horror music, then a virtual reality dark basement. Detection was measured as a signal-detection criterion on a biological motion task, an auditory agent detection task and a Heider-and-Simmel-style geometrical figures task. No manipulation raised the bias towards detecting agents. In Experiment 1a the threatening pictures left the criterion untouched, F(1,29) = 0.13, p = .717, while the noise manipulation worked as intended on sensitivity, F(1.61, 46.62) = 24.63, p < .001. The more awkward result is the direction of the criterion itself. In every experiment using human agent detection, participants leant towards judging that no agent was present, which is the opposite of a hair trigger. Only the geometrical figures task produced a bias towards perceiving intentionality, and the paper describes it as small and close to zero.

Pooling the four experiments that carried questionnaires, 130 participants, an analysis of covariance found neither religiosity nor the Revised Paranormal Belief Scale related to the response bias. The paranormal scale came out at F = 1.40, p = .239. The one covariate that did predict a bias towards detecting agents was the Negativity Bias Scale, F = 6.79, p = .010, and it survived entry on its own, F(1,126) = 4.10, p = .045.

Tratner, Shackelford, Zeigler-Hill, Vonk and McDonald tried again in virtual reality with 107 students. The task worked as a task: most participants reported an agent at least once where none existed. It did not work as a test of the theory. False detection correlated r = .17, p = .08 with belief in supernatural agents and r = .25, p = .008 with overall supernatural belief, which their Bonferroni-corrected threshold of .006 rejects. The one correlation that cleared the threshold was with belief in Feng Shui, r = .35, p = .001, which the authors call unanticipated and warn may be a Type I error.

The verdict is mixed rather than failed because van Elk's 2013 result runs the other way, and because the two sides use different populations and different belief scales. What has not survived is the causal prediction. Threat does not raise agent detection, supernatural priming does not raise it, and the individual-difference link that does appear attaches to paranormal belief and to negativity bias rather than to religion.

study.cite: Maij, D. L. R., van Schie, H. T., & van Elk, M. (2019). The boundary conditions of the hypersensitive agency detection device: an empirical investigation of agency detection in threatening situations. Religion, Brain & Behavior, 9(1), 23-51.

limits:
No effect sizes appear in the structured fields. The two sides report a signal-detection criterion in an analysis of covariance and a zero-order correlation between click counts and questionnaire scores, and pairing them would invent a comparison neither paper makes. Nothing here is a like-for-like replication of anything else. Every study named uses its own task and its own belief instrument, and a null on a biological motion criterion does not settle what a virtual forest would show.

Two statistics in the Maij paper are internally inconsistent and are not quoted on this page. Its Table 2 gives the religiosity covariate as F = 1.16 with p = .078, and Experiment 1b's criterion as F(1,31) = 0.04 with p = .178. Neither p value is consistent with its own F and degrees of freedom. The figures used above are the ones that are.

Sample sizes are small throughout, and the recruited figure is not the analysed one. Maij's headline 233 is a recruitment total. Experiment 1b excluded one of 33, Experiment 2b excluded five of 63, and Experiment 3 kept 37 of the 45 it recruited. The fMRI study had 12 believers and 11 skeptics. Tratner's authors excluded six people and say their own 107 may have inflated the unexpected Feng Shui result. Maij and colleagues also note that their samples were barely religious, with mean religiosity between 1.4 and 2.6 on a seven-point scale, which limits what a null on the belief correlation can mean.

The search covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, the Open Science Framework and the table of contents of Religion, Brain & Behavior volume 9, issue 1, on 21 September 2026. No Many Labs project, registered replication report or meta-analysis of agent detection was found. Andersen's virtual reality study is the only preregistered study among those named here, and its participant count is still missing. The publisher answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall notice. The Aarhus Pure record marks the article restricted access and the Bielefeld record marks it closed, and neither holds a file; both were read through their OAI routes, which the guarded pages do not cover. The abstract gives no sample size, so the number is left off rather than guessed. Guthrie's 1993 book was verified as a 1993 Oxford University Press title through Open Library and is cited from the description in Maij and colleagues rather than from its own pages. Barrett's 2000 article was read only as its Europe PMC abstract.

An earlier brief for this entry named a 2017 Royal Society Open Science paper with seven studies and more than 1,800 participants finding no relationship between agency detection and religious belief. No such paper exists. A Crossref search restricted to the journal's ISSN on 21 September 2026 again returned nothing on agency detection. The nearest real papers are Maij, van Schie and van Elk's six experiments, and Maij, van Harreveld, Gervais, Schrag, Mohr and van Elk's five studies in PLOS ONE, whose abstract gives over 67,000 participants in total. That paper tested mentalizing rather than agent detection. It reports the empathy quotient and the autism-spectrum quotient as unpredictive of belief in supernatural agents in the Netherlands, Switzerland and the United States, with a curvilinear effect in the United States, while credibility enhancing displays predicted belief strongly.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to treat one claim as evidence for the other. That people attribute purpose to moving shapes is settled; Heider and Simmel got it from all but one of 34 women in 1944 and it reproduces in every undergraduate class since. That this tendency explains why anyone believes in gods is a different claim with a poor record, and quoting the triangles in support of it proves nothing.

The second error is to describe the detector as hair-triggered on the strength of signal-detection studies. Those studies measure a criterion, and the criterion in Maij's biological motion and auditory tasks sat on the conservative side: people were more inclined to say no agent was there. False detections are common in tasks that ask people to interpret motion or to hunt for beings in a virtual wood. They are not the default in tasks that ask whether a figure is present.

A third is to read the failures as a verdict on cognitive science of religion. What has failed is a specific causal prediction about threat and a specific correlation with belief. Barrett's own framework, as Maij and colleagues summarise it, treats agent detection as a contributing factor that merely encourages belief and needs mentalizing to do the rest.

A fourth is to run religious and paranormal belief together. Van Elk's 2013 paper found illusory agency detection strongly related to psi, spiritualism, precognition and superstition, and unrelated to traditional religious belief and belief in witchcraft. An entry that reports a link without saying which belief was measured has lost the finding.

The field has largely moved to a different framing. Andersen argued in 2019 that predictive coding accounts for agency detection better than a dedicated module does, and his virtual reality data put expectation far ahead of sensory ambiguity. Guthrie replied in the same issue, in a commentary called 'Prediction and feedback may constrain but do not stop anthropomorphism'. Barrett did not reply. A search of his publications found a response in the same journal, online in 2017 and printed in 2018, but it answers Kim Sterelny rather than the empirical work described here.
